extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism, editors of Coleridge/Wordsworth, and scholars of religious and poetic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for judging religious doctrines, poetic works, and critical practice (as set out in an editor's/introduction's defense of Coleridge). Emphasizes moral/practical bearings, poetic ends, and editorials standards for preparing texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge revealed truth by practical grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Revealed truth are to be judged of by us, as far as they are grounds of practice or in some way connected with our moral and spiritual interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess doctrines by their capacity for practical application and their relation to the moral and spiritual life of people — the 'life, the substance, the hope, the love' of faith are derivatives from the practical, moral, and spiritual nature of man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion must have a moral origin and independent evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion must have a moral origin, so far at least, that the evidence of its doctrines, like the truths of abstract science, be wholly independent of will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate religious claims for their moral grounding and for evidence that does not depend on mere volition or affect; religion should improve the faculties of man and relate to the main end of human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test creeds by moral/spiritual bearings rather than mere logical precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not try a religious creed according to logical and technical precision alone, without regard to its deeper moral and spiritual bearings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism that focuses only on technical exactness risks missing whether a tenet, in ordinary form, conflicts with conscience or practical reason; moral considerations often motivated departures from orthodoxy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the speculative mind's limits in judging practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: The speculative mind is ill qualified to judge truly of doctrines whose test is practical application and relation to appointed ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers inclined to pure speculation may prefer shallow or fantastical views; practical consequences and lived results are essential tests that speculation alone cannot supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrines should be assessed by tendencies and characteristics, not only intellectual handling
rubrics_metrics.description: A creed should be considered in respect to its moral characteristics and tendencies, not merely in respect to logical and technical precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating belief-systems, consider how they shape moral character and spiritual life; avoid reducing assessment to purely abstract or technical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensuous forms may preserve and contain spiritual ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: A sensuous, 'childlike' conception (e.g., ancient notions of Eucharist) can preserve the substance of a spiritual idea in a 'cocoon' until the spiritual doctrine is developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss sensuous or ancient formulations as merely absurd; they may have preserved the underlying spiritual reality and made it accessible to faith until clearer doctrine emerges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superstition is disguised infidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: Superstition is not a debased form of faith but a disguised infidelity, since men become superstitious inasmuch as they are sensuous and dark slaves by their own compulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish legitimate religious feeling and form from superstition; critique practices that substitute sensuous dependence for reflective faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not establish faith on feeling and fancy apart from reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Refuse to establish faith on feeling and fancy, apart from reflection, and to adopt the maxim that forms of doctrine associated with religious ideas are to be received implicitly without examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious belief should be open to reflection and examination; implicit, unexamined acceptance of doctrines that stifle truth is cautioned against.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious and moral writing should aim at practical usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole aim of moral and religious writings is usefulness — the regulation of action and the furtherance of man's well being here and hereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess such writings for whether they produce practical moral improvement and useful guidance for conduct, not merely abstruse theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's final aim: benefit man morally (poetry as visible language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is a visible language whose final aim is to benefit man by means of delight, for his moral and religious well‑being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poetry by its capacity to contribute to human well‑being and moral improvement; if religious or moral writings (and by extension poetry) lack practical wisdom, they are empty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should address the common heart and universal reason
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet who addresses the common heart and universal reason (e.g., Wordsworth) is preferable to one whose work has a narrow, self‑contained world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value poems that engage broadly with human feeling and thought over works that display merely elegant, inward‑turned fancy; breadth and capacity to engage general hearts and minds are positive qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poems ought to exhibit freshness, depth, and capacity to interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems should have freshness of thought and feeling and be 'deep' enough to interest the heart and mind; examples include listed Wordsworth poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess specific poems for their immediate effects on readers: whether they show power as poetry, freshness, and the capacity to move and command respect; a poem can be understood and respected even if not deeply enjoyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical judgments must be determined by specific results and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of poetic merit are so fine and complex that they must be determined, as specific cases, by the effects produced and experience rather than by rigid rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should look to the actual influence and effects of a work on readership and poetic sensibility; specific results and experience trump mechanical application of rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid partisan or personal attacks in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical warfare carried on with personal remarks and party‑spirit discredits the critique; personal anecdotes or lampoons may be inaccurate and injure a good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess criticism for impartiality; avoid letting political or personal animus determine aesthetic judgments. Editors may suppress personal remarks as anomalies when preparing editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial principle: minimal interference and suppression of personal remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: As an editor preparing an author's work for the press, abstain from changing the text as far as the sense is concerned, alter only to remove unquestionable mistakes of fact, and suppress personal passages thought to be anomalies or inaccurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editing posthumous or historical texts, preserve authorial sense, correct clear factual errors only, and omit personal or incendiary passages that the author likely would not have reprinted; explain such suppressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual statement of doctrine should be intelligible and distinct; spiritual idea positive and certain
rubrics_metrics.description: The spiritual ideas contained in doctrine ought to be positive and certain; the intellectual statement of the doctrine should be intelligible and distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between the experiential/spiritual content of belief (should have positive certainty) and the intellectual formulation (should be clear and distinct); evaluate both aspects when assessing doctrinal statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemplation is a legitimate calling and not necessarily a lack of practical wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: A life of contemplation and thinking for thinking's sake is not necessarily inaction or unfitness to be a moral preceptor; contemplation can be the 'calling to which his Maker called him.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a thinker or writer, do not equate contemplative life with uselessness; consider whether their thought had practical ends or benefitted others even if their primary activity was reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism should distinguish between appearances and substantive merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment formed by appearances (or by party‑tinted spectacles) may misrepresent a poet's merit; careful, competent criticism must look beyond surface presentation to substantive qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hasty dismissal based on polemical accounts; critics should read works attentively and judge by their intrinsic poetic powers rather than partisan portrayals.
